planting.note: Direct sow into lean, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed; Picotee's ruffled bicolor petals show best when the plant isn't pushed with rich soil or heavy fertilizer.

directions: Picotee is an old cottage-garden cosmos strain grown for its distinctive petals: creamy white to pale pink with a fine crimson-maroon edge that darkens toward the petal tip, giving each bloom a hand-painted, feathered look. The plant carries the same lacy, thread-like foliage and airy, wind-tolerant habit typical of the species, and its slender stems make excellent long-lasting cut flowers. Because seedlings vary somewhat in the depth of the picotee edging, growing a full row from a packet gives a pleasing range from barely-tinted white through deeply rimmed rose. Regular deadheading keeps new buds forming from midsummer until the first hard frost.

planting.note: Direct sow after frost risk passes into lean soil; Daydream is a Sensation-type selection grown for its pale petal color and contrasting dark eye rather than a separately bred dwarf series.

directions: Daydream carries the classic wide, flat-faced flower of the Sensation strain, but in a distinctive soft blush-pink that pales almost to white at the petal tips while a narrow band of deeper rose-maroon rings the central disc, creating a soft target pattern rather than a solid color. The finely divided, fern-like foliage and tall, airy stems are typical Cosmos bipinnatus, tolerating poor soil and drought far better than richly fed beds. Its gentler coloring blends easily with both pastel and saturated companions in a cutting garden or mixed border, and it draws bees, hoverflies, and small butterflies over a long summer bloom period. Cutting stems for arrangements or deadheading spent flowers both encourage continued branching and bloom.

planting.note: Direct sow into lean, well-drained soil after frost danger passes; Purity's pure white flowers show soil splash and mildew more readily than colored types, so good air circulation and dry foliage help keep petals clean.

directions: Purity is a long-standing selection grown for flowers that open a truly clean white, without the pale-pink or cream cast that many other 'white' cosmos show, set against a soft yellow center disc. The tall, finely cut, almost feathery foliage and open, airy branching are typical of Cosmos bipinnatus, and the same lean-soil, low-water preferences apply — overly rich beds produce lush leaves and fewer blooms. Because the flat, white flowers show up strongly at dusk, Purity is a favorite for moon gardens and evening-viewed borders, and its stems hold up well in cut arrangements. Deadheading through the season keeps plants flowering from early summer to frost.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; Sunny Red was bred as a dwarf, uniform bedding selection considerably shorter than heirloom sulfur cosmos strains.

directions: Sunny Red was one of the earliest dwarf breeding breakthroughs in Cosmos sulphureus, bred to hold the species' vivid, heat-loving orange-red single flowers on a compact, well-branched plant well under knee height rather than the loose, lanky habit of older sulfur cosmos strains. It flowers unusually early and continues nonstop through the hottest, most humid part of summer when many bedding annuals stall, needing no pinching or staking to stay tidy. Like other sulfur cosmos, it thrives in poor, dry soil and full sun and is a strong draw for butterflies and small pollinators. Its short, uniform habit made it a natural fit for mass bedding and container plantings where taller cosmos varieties would overwhelm the design.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; Sunny Gold shares Sunny Red's dwarf, compact habit but in a rich golden-orange color.

directions: Sunny Gold is the golden-orange companion to the dwarf Sunny Red sulfur cosmos, bred for the same compact, well-branched habit that stays well under two feet tall while producing abundant single flowers over a long, heat-tolerant season. It shares the species' preference for poor, lean, well-drained soil and struggles with excess fertility, which produces soft foliage growth at the expense of flowers. Because it stays shorter and sturdier than heirloom sulfur cosmos strains, Sunny Gold needs no staking and holds up well in open, windy sites or container plantings. Deadheading extends bloom, though sulfur cosmos also self-seeds readily where the soil stays warm into fall.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed; like other Double Click colors, Rose Bonbon takes longer to reach its first flush of bloom than single-flowered cosmos types.

directions: Double Click Rose Bonbon carries the same fully double, ruffled flower form as its Cranberry and Mother of Pearl series-mates, but in a clear, saturated bubblegum-pink that reads as a solid color rather than the blended shades seen elsewhere in the series. The dense, multi-petaled blooms resemble small dahlias more than the flat, single daisy form typical of Cosmos bipinnatus, and the long, sturdy stems make it a strong performer in cutting gardens. Like the rest of the Double Click line from PanAmerican Seed, it blooms later than single cosmos but produces continuously from midsummer to frost once started, and it tolerates the same lean soil and drought that stresses richer-fed annuals. Successive plantings a few weeks apart extend fresh-cut production through the season.
sources: PanAmerican Seed — Double Click Cosmos Series Introduction
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Annual Flowers for Full Sun

planting.note: Direct sow into lean soil after frost danger passes; Antiquity's dusty, fading petal color develops its full antique tone as flowers age over several days rather than at first opening.

directions: Antiquity is a dwarf, compact cosmos selection grown for its unusual fading color: semi-double flowers open a warm dusty rose and gradually soften through mauve to a soft creamy tan as they age, so a single plant carries several shades at once. Its shorter, well-branched habit sets it apart from tall heirloom Cosmos bipinnatus strains and suits it to borders and containers where floppy, leggy cosmos would need staking. The muted, antique color palette pairs easily with dried-flower and cut-flower designs, since the aging blooms hold their softened tones well after cutting. Like other cosmos, it flowers best in lean, well-drained soil and needs no regular fertilizing to perform through a long summer season.
sources: Thompson & Morgan — Cosmos Antiquity Grower Information
